opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think scaling laws matter for long-horizon evaluations because they turn evaluation from a snapshot into a forecast.

If you test a model on a long, multi-step task, like a real software engineering project or a research workflow that takes hours or days, you get a data point about what that model can do today. What you really want to know is where the trend is heading. Scaling laws give you that lens. If performance on these tasks improves predictably with compute, data, or inference-time reasoning, you can start to anticipate when models will cross important thresholds, instead of being surprised after the fact.

That matters for two reasons. The first is preparedness and safety. Many of the capabilities we care most about, like autonomously carrying out complex tasks, conducting research, or acting in the world over extended periods, are long-horizon by nature. If you can see a capability coming, you have time to build the right mitigations and policies before the model arrives, rather than scrambling afterward.

The second is that long-horizon tasks are where real economic value lives. Most meaningful work isn't a single question and answer. It's sustained effort with planning, error correction, and judgment. A common way of framing this is to measure the length of task a model can reliably complete. If that length keeps growing on a predictable curve, it tells you a lot about how AI will actually change work.

There's an honest caveat. Long-horizon evals are expensive and noisy, and progress on them may not always be smooth. Sometimes capabilities seem to appear suddenly because a model has to get many steps right in a row, and small improvements in per-step reliability compound into big jumps in end-to-end success. So part of the job is designing evaluations with enough granularity, through partial credit and intermediate checkpoints, that you can see the underlying trend even when the headline number looks like a step function.

So to me, scaling laws are what make these evaluations useful for decisions. They help us move from "here's what the model did" to "here's what's likely coming, and here's how we should prepare."

r001.rationale: The response says scaling laws can forecast trends and anticipate capability thresholds, but it does not explain that shorter-horizon evaluation results predict longer-horizon performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that scaling laws are what let us turn evaluation from a snapshot into a forecast, and for long-horizon tasks that distinction really matters.

When you evaluate a model on a short task, you get a number, and that number is useful on its own. But when the tasks are long, multi-step, agentic things, where the model has to plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and sustain coherence over hours of work, a single number tells you much less. The variance is huge. Success often hinges on whether the model gets past one bottleneck step, and small improvements in per-step reliability compound into very large differences in whether the whole task gets done. So if you only look at today's model, you can easily conclude "it can't do this," and be completely wrong six months later.

Scaling laws give you the trend line. If you can measure how performance on these long-horizon tasks moves as a function of compute, or model size, or the amount of task-relevant training, you can start asking the questions that actually matter for safety and deployment: how far away are we from the model being able to complete a week-long research project autonomously? At what point does it cross the threshold where it could meaningfully accelerate someone working on something dangerous? Those are forecasting questions, and you can't answer them without a scaling relationship.

The other reason I care about this is that long-horizon evals are expensive and slow to build. You're constructing realistic environments, you're having experts write and grade tasks, sometimes you're running things for many hours per sample. You cannot afford to build a new eval from scratch every time a new model shows up. If you understand the scaling behavior, you can design the eval once, with enough headroom and enough difficulty gradient that it stays informative across several generations of models. You're essentially designing a measurement instrument that you know will still be in range as the thing you're measuring grows.

And then there's a more subtle point, which is that scaling behavior itself is a signal. When a capability scales smoothly, you can plan around it. When it doesn't, when you see a jump, or a plateau, or performance that depends heavily on something other than raw scale, like scaffolding or post-training, that tells you something important about what's driving the capability. For long-horizon work especially, a lot of the gains have come from training the model to persist, to check its own work, to use tools well. Separating "this got better because the model got bigger" from "this got better because we taught it a specific skill" is really important if you want to make credible predictions.

So I'd put it this way: scaling laws are what make long-horizon evaluation predictive rather than merely descriptive. And for the kinds of decisions we're trying to inform, about preparedness, about when to add mitigations, about how fast things are moving, predictive is the whole point.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling laws forecast long-horizon performance from trends across compute, model size, or training. It does not clearly say that shorter-horizon evaluation results can be used to predict longer-horizon evaluation performance.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling laws are important because long-horizon evaluations are expensive, and we want to understand more than just whether a model can finish a particular task today. We want to understand how that ability changes as models improve.

On a long task, a model has to make a sequence of decisions, keep track of what it’s doing, and recover when something goes wrong. Being a little better at each step could translate into a much higher chance of completing the whole task. But errors can also compound, so that relationship isn’t necessarily straightforward.

If we can measure those trends across models and task lengths, we can start to make predictions about what future models might accomplish and design evaluations that will still be informative when they arrive. The key is to test those predictions, rather than assume that better performance on short tasks automatically means reliable performance over longer horizons.

r001.rationale: The response says trends across models and task lengths may help predict what future models could accomplish, but it does not explain predicting longer-horizon evaluation performance from shorter-horizon evaluation results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling laws are important because long-horizon evaluations are expensive, and we want to understand how capabilities change as models improve. If we can measure performance across different model scales and task lengths, we can start to see whether progress is predictable and where that predictability breaks down.

A model might be very reliable at individual steps but still struggle to complete a task that requires hundreds of them. Small errors accumulate, and recovering from those errors becomes part of the task. So it’s useful to look beyond a single success rate and ask how reliability changes with the length of the horizon.

That can help us design evaluations that remain informative as models get better, and decide where to spend our evaluation effort. But I’d treat those scaling trends as hypotheses to test, rather than substitutes for actually measuring long-horizon performance.

r001.rationale: The response says to measure performance across model scales and task lengths to look for predictable trends, but it does not clearly state that shorter-horizon results can predict longer-horizon evaluation performance.
